checks.prompt: A telephony product on this cloud provider needs spoken prompts in twelve languages, precise control over pauses and how phone numbers and dates are read out, audio encoded for a phone network, and access governed by the organisation's existing identity policies. A second team wants a character voice cloned from an actor's recording. Which team does this service fit, and what is the honest limitation for the other?
checks.explanation: This service's strengths are breadth and plumbing rather than peak expressiveness: a wide multilingual catalogue, a markup language that gives real control over pauses, emphasis and how dates, numbers and telephone strings are spoken, telephony-native encodings with device-tuned audio profiles, and the cloud's identity, network-control and compliance machinery. The limitation worth knowing before you commit is that there is no general voice cloning — you pick from the catalogue, and the custom-voice offering is gated and enterprise-only.
options: The first. It offers a broad catalogue across roughly fifty languages, a markup language giving explicit control over pauses, emphasis and how dates, numbers and telephone strings are spoken, native telephony encodings with device-tuned audio profiles, and the provider's own identity and compliance plumbing. The second team is out of luck here: there is no general voice-cloning product — you choose from the provider's catalogue, and a custom-voice programme exists only as a gated enterprise offering
The second. Cloning from a sample is the service's headline feature, while telephony prompts are better served by a self-hosted engine because phone encodings are not supported
Both. Cloning is available on the standard tiers, and the markup language covers telephony encoding as well
Neither. The service synthesises only plain text with no markup, so the pause and number-reading requirements need client-side audio editing, and cloning is unavailable

checks.prompt: Describe this service as a vending machine with a quality dial. Name the three orthogonal parts of every request and say what each decides. Explain what the voice name encodes beyond identity and why that matters commercially. Then explain the one structural limit on a synchronous call and what you do about it for long-form content.
checks.expected: A correct answer must set out the three parts. The input is WHAT to say: exactly one of a plain string or a marked-up document, the markup giving access to pauses, emphasis, instructions for how to interpret dates, numbers and telephone strings, phoneme overrides, prosody and timing marks. The voice selection is WHO says it: a language tag plus optionally a specific voice name, with a requested gender used only when no name is given. The audio configuration is HOW the result is shaped and encoded: the encoding, the speaking rate, the pitch, the volume gain, the sample rate, and device-tuned audio profiles. The voice name point must be made: the name encodes the QUALITY TIER as well as the identity, running from a cheap basic tier through neural tiers to a premium long-form tier and the newest generative one — so choosing a voice is choosing a price, and the difference between the cheapest and the most expensive tier is roughly fortyfold, which makes picking a fancy voice by habit a budget decision rather than a taste one. The structural limit must be named precisely: a synchronous call accepts at most about five thousand BYTES of input, markup included, so long documents must either be chunked by the caller or sent through the separate asynchronous long-audio interface, which writes its output to cloud storage and supports only the uncompressed encoding. Noting that billing counts every input character including markup, so verbose markup multiplies cost, is a plus.

checks.prompt: Two teams report problems. One set the pitch parameter to 200 expecting a value in hertz and got an error; they then set the speaking rate to 200 and got an error too. Another team's synthesis of Japanese prompts is rejected as too long even though each prompt is under two thousand characters. What are the mechanisms?
checks.explanation: Two independent details that both bite. The shaping controls are on unrelated scales: a semitone shift within about plus or minus twenty for pitch, and a multiplier of normal speed between roughly a quarter and four for rate — confusing them produces either an error or comically wrong audio. And the synchronous size limit counts encoded BYTES rather than characters, so a script in a language whose characters occupy three bytes each reaches the ceiling at about a third of the character count, which is exactly the surprise here.
options: The two shaping parameters are on different scales entirely: pitch is a shift in semitones within roughly plus or minus twenty, and speaking rate is a multiplier of normal speed between about a quarter and four times — neither is a hertz value and neither is a percentage. And the length limit is expressed in BYTES of encoded input, not characters, so a script in a language whose characters take three bytes each hits the limit at roughly a third of the character count
Pitch is indeed in hertz but capped at 100, and speaking rate is a percentage capped at 100; the Japanese rejection means the language tag was wrong, since per-language limits vary
Both parameters accept any value but are silently clamped, so the errors must come from the encoding; and the Japanese rejection is a quota problem rather than a size problem

Pitch and speaking rate are both multipliers with the same range, so 200 is out of bounds for both; and the Japanese rejection happens because non-Latin scripts must use the asynchronous interface regardless of length

checks.prompt: Model the request contract and the pricing arithmetic — nothing is sent. Define `TIER` mapping `"Standard"` to price 4.0 per million characters with 4000000 free, `"Wavenet"` and `"Neural2"` to 16.0 with 1000000 free, `"Studio"` to 160.0 with 100000 free, and `"Chirp3-HD"` to 30.0 with none free; `ENCODINGS = {"MP3", "LINEAR16", "OGG_OPUS", "MULAW", "ALAW"}`; and `MAX_REQUEST_BYTES = 5000`. Write `tier_of(voice_name)` reading the tier out of a hyphen-separated name: the third component when it is a known tier, `"Chirp3-HD"` when the third and fourth are `"Chirp3"` and `"HD"`, and `ValueError` for a name with fewer than four components or an unrecognised tier. Write `monthly_cost(chars, tier)` returning the characters beyond that tier's free allowance, divided by a million and multiplied by its rate, raising `ValueError` for an unknown tier. Write `billable_characters(text=None, ssml=None)` and `input_bytes(text=None, ssml=None)`, each requiring EXACTLY one of the two and otherwise raising `ValueError`, returning respectively the character count and the UTF-8 byte count. Write `validate_audio_config(config)` returning the config, raising `ValueError` unless its `audioEncoding` is known, its `speakingRate` (default 1.0) is between 0.25 and 4.0, and its `pitch` (default 0.0) is between −20 and 20. Write `build_request(language_code, text=None, ssml=None, name=None, ssml_gender=None, audio_config=None)` returning `{"input", "voice", "audioConfig"}`: raise `ValueError` if the input exceeds `MAX_REQUEST_BYTES`, with a message mentioning the long audio interface; the input carries whichever of the two forms was given; the voice always carries `languageCode`, carries `name` when given — which must start with the language code and a hyphen, and must name a known tier — and otherwise carries `ssmlGender` when that was given; and the audio config defaults to MP3 and is validated. Do not mutate the caller's audio config. Standard library only.
checks.explanation: Three commercial facts are encoded here as code. The voice name carries the price tier, so two names differing by one word differ by forty times in cost — reading the tier out of the name is how you know what a call will cost before you make it. Free allowances are per tier and only the overage is billed, which is why the same volume is free on one tier and costs real money on another. And markup is input: the marked-up version of a twelve-character sentence bills for forty-nine characters, so verbose markup is a multiplier on the bill rather than a free convenience. The size assertions carry the subtlest point — the synchronous limit counts encoded bytes, so seventeen hundred characters in a three-byte-per-character script is already over the ceiling while five thousand Latin characters is not. Finally, note that a requested gender is dropped when a specific voice was named: it only decides anything when the choice was left open.
checks.test:
# The voice name IS the price tier -- reading it is how you know what a call costs.
assert tier_of("en-US-Standard-C") == "Standard"
assert tier_of("en-US-Neural2-F") == "Neural2"
assert tier_of("ja-JP-Wavenet-A") == "Wavenet"
assert tier_of("en-US-Studio-O") == "Studio"
assert tier_of("en-US-Chirp3-HD-Charon") == "Chirp3-HD"
for bad in ("en-US-Fancy-A", "en-US-Neural2", "rubbish"):
    try:
        tier_of(bad)
    except ValueError:
        continue
    raise AssertionError(f"{bad!r} must be refused")

# Two voices that differ by one word in their name differ by forty times in price.
assert TIER["Studio"]["per_1m"] / TIER["Standard"]["per_1m"] == 40.0

# Each tier has its own free monthly allowance, and only the overage is billed.
assert monthly_cost(200_000, "Standard") == 0.0
assert monthly_cost(200_000, "Neural2") == 0.0
assert monthly_cost(200_000, "Studio") == 16.0
assert monthly_cost(200_000, "Chirp3-HD") == 6.0
assert monthly_cost(4_000_000, "Standard") == 0.0
assert monthly_cost(5_000_000, "Standard") == 4.0
assert monthly_cost(0, "Studio") == 0.0
try:
    monthly_cost(10, "Premium")
except ValueError:
    pass
else:
    raise AssertionError("an unknown tier must be refused")

# Every character of the input is billed, and markup is input.
plain = "Hello world."
markup = "<speak>Hello <break time='300ms'/> world.</speak>"
assert billable_characters(text=plain) == 12
assert billable_characters(ssml=markup) == 49, billable_characters(ssml=markup)
assert billable_characters(ssml=markup) > billable_characters(text=plain) * 4
for bad in ({}, {"text": "a", "ssml": "<speak/>"}):
    try:
        billable_characters(**bad)
    except ValueError:
        continue
    raise AssertionError(f"{bad} must be refused")

# The synchronous limit is in BYTES, not characters, which is why text that looks
# comfortably short in a non-Latin script can still be rejected.
assert input_bytes(text="hello") == 5
assert input_bytes(text="héllo") == 6
assert input_bytes(text="こんにちは") == 15
build_request("en-US", text="x" * 5000)
for oversize in ("x" * 5001, "é" * 2600, "あ" * 1700):
    try:
        build_request("en-US", text=oversize)
    except ValueError as exc:
        assert "long audio" in str(exc), exc
    else:
        raise AssertionError("an over-long input must be refused")
# ...and that last one is only 1700 characters.
assert len("あ" * 1700) == 1700 and input_bytes(text="あ" * 1700) == 5100

request = build_request("en-US", text="Hello.", name="en-US-Neural2-F")
assert request["input"] == {"text": "Hello."}
assert request["voice"] == {"languageCode": "en-US", "name": "en-US-Neural2-F"}
assert request["audioConfig"] == {"audioEncoding": "MP3"}
assert "ssml" not in request["input"]

assert build_request("en-US", ssml="<speak>Hi.</speak>")["input"] == \
    {"ssml": "<speak>Hi.</speak>"}

# The requested gender only decides anything when no specific voice was named.
chosen = build_request("en-US", text="Hi.", name="en-US-Studio-O",
                       ssml_gender="FEMALE")
assert "ssmlGender" not in chosen["voice"], chosen
unnamed = build_request("en-US", text="Hi.", ssml_gender="FEMALE")
assert unnamed["voice"] == {"languageCode": "en-US", "ssmlGender": "FEMALE"}

# A voice that does not belong to the requested language is refused up front.
try:
    build_request("en-US", text="Hi.", name="ja-JP-Neural2-B")
except ValueError:
    pass
else:
    raise AssertionError("a mismatched voice and language must be refused")

# The two shaping controls are on different scales, and each has a real range.
config = {"audioEncoding": "LINEAR16", "speakingRate": 1.5, "pitch": -4.0}
assert build_request("en-US", text="Hi.", audio_config=config)["audioConfig"] == config
for bad in ({"audioEncoding": "FLAC"}, {"audioEncoding": "MP3", "speakingRate": 0.1},
            {"audioEncoding": "MP3", "speakingRate": 5.0},
            {"audioEncoding": "MP3", "pitch": 24.0},
            {"audioEncoding": "MP3", "pitch": -30.0}):
    try:
        validate_audio_config(bad)
    except ValueError:
        continue
    raise AssertionError(f"{bad} must be refused")
for good in ({"audioEncoding": "MULAW"}, {"audioEncoding": "ALAW"},
             {"audioEncoding": "OGG_OPUS", "speakingRate": 4.0, "pitch": 20.0},
             {"audioEncoding": "MP3", "speakingRate": 0.25, "pitch": -20.0}):
    validate_audio_config(good)

# The caller's dict is not modified by validation or by building the request.
original = {"audioEncoding": "MP3"}
build_request("en-US", text="Hi.", audio_config=original)
assert original == {"audioEncoding": "MP3"}

checks.prompt: A new project fails in sequence: first with an error about default credentials, then, once those are configured, with a permission denial, and finally — after that is resolved — the audio arrives but the phone system it feeds plays static. What are the three causes and the fixes?
checks.explanation: Three setup traps that arrive in exactly this order. Missing default credentials is the first: point the environment at a service-account key or authenticate for local development. A permission denial next is almost always the service not being enabled on the project or a missing role — and billing has to be enabled even to use the free allowance, which surprises people. And the static at the end is an encoding mismatch: a phone network wants a telephony encoding at its own low sample rate, further signal processing wants uncompressed samples, and the web wants a compressed format.
options: The credentials error means application default credentials are not configured — point the environment at a service-account key or authenticate locally for development. The permission denial usually means the service is not enabled on the project, or the service account lacks the role — and note that synthesis requires billing to be enabled even inside the free allowance. The static is an encoding mismatch: a phone network wants a telephony encoding at its own low sample rate, not the compressed web default
All three are the same misconfigured credential, since the client falls back to an anonymous mode that returns a placeholder tone; a single valid key resolves them
The credentials error is expected on first run and self-heals; the permission denial means the character quota is exhausted; and the static means the speaking rate exceeded its range

The credentials error means the client library version is too old; the permission denial means the chosen voice is not available in the project's region; and the static means the markup contained an unsupported tag

checks.prompt: Compare this service with a naturalness-leading specialist vendor, the equivalent services from the other two major clouds, and a self-hosted open engine. Say what each wins on and what it costs. Then advise a company already on this cloud, building an accessibility read-aloud feature covering thirty languages with an expected two million characters a month, who also want a signature brand voice for their advertising. Say what you would use for each half and what you would watch on the bill.
checks.expected: A correct answer must position all four. This service wins on breadth of languages and voices, real markup control, telephony-native encodings and device profiles, and the cloud's own identity, network-control and compliance machinery, at the cost of being less expressive than the naturalness leader, having no general voice cloning, per-character billing and being cloud-only. The specialist vendor wins on best-in-class naturalness and instant voice cloning, at the cost of price at the quality tier and far fewer enterprise controls. The other clouds' services are comparable in quality and are the right answer when you are native to those platforms rather than this one. The self-hosted open engine wins on running offline with no per-use bill and audio never leaving the machine, at the cost of running the operations yourself and quality that trails hosted options. The recommendation must split the two halves: the read-aloud feature belongs here — the team is already on this cloud, thirty languages is exactly the breadth argument, and accessibility benefits from the markup control; the brand voice belongs with the specialist vendor, because a signature cloned voice is the one thing this service does not offer outside a gated programme. What to watch on the bill must be concrete: choosing the cheapest tier that sounds good enough, since the voice name is the price tier and the premium tiers cost many times more; keeping markup tight, because every markup character is billed; and staying aware of per-tier free allowances against a two-million-character monthly volume, which exceeds the neural tiers' allowance and would be free on the cheapest tier. Noting the five-thousand-byte synchronous limit and the asynchronous long-audio path for anything long-form is a plus.
